Created in 1963, 'Whirlpool' by Krishna Reddy is universally acclaimed as a global milestone in 20th-century graphic art. Working as co-director alongside Stanley William Hayter at the renowned 'Atelier 17' printmaking workshop in Paris, Reddy revolutionized the medium by inventing the process of simultaneous multi-color viscosity printing on a single metal intaglio plate. Created around 1940 by master artist Jamini Roy, 'Mother and Child' is a seminal monument of modern Indian folk revivalism. Trained initially in British academic realism and having experimented with the Bengal wash style, Roy made a radical break around 1921 to return to the living folk craft traditions of his native Bankura district in rural Bengal. Drawing inspiration from Kalighat scroll paintings (patuas) and village terracotta toys, Roy eliminated academic photographic shading and perspective. In 'Mother and Child', the mother tenderly cradles her infant in a sweeping protective embrace. Both figures are rendered with bold, fluid, unbroken black contour lines and oversized, expressive almond-shaped eyes that dominate their serene faces. Roy rejected expensive imported oil paints, grinding his own natural pigments from alluvial river clay, turmeric, chalk, and soot mixed with tree gum, creating a flat, democratic, and universally accessible art form, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.

The National Flag of India is a horizontal tricolour of three equal rectangular panels: India Saffron (Kesari) at the top, White in the middle, and India Green at the bottom. Painted in 1988 in oil on canvas, 'Mother Teresa' by Maqbool Fida (M.F.) Husain is a monumental modern tribute to universal compassion. Husain, who co-founded the revolutionary Progressive Artists' Group (PAG) in Bombay in December 1947 alongside Souza, Raza, and Ara, sought to create an aggressive, internationally relevant modern Indian art free from colonial academicism. In 'Mother Teresa', Husain deliberately renders the saint's face as a dark, featureless void: she is identified solely by the iconic white cotton saree with three blue borders worn by the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta. The drape of the saree curves across the composition like a monumental cathedral arch, cradling an abandoned, sick child across her lap in a powerful visual echo of Michelangelo's 'Pietà'. By omitting her physical features, Husain elevated Mother Teresa from an individual historical nun into a timeless, universal embodiment of selfless motherhood, divine grace, and compassionate sanctuary, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.

Painted around 1900 in oil on canvas by Raja Ravi Varma, 'Rama Vanquishing the Pride of the Ocean' is an epic landmark of modern Indian academic realism. Based on the Yuddha Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, the painting depicts Lord Rama standing upon dark, storm-tossed coastal rocks, fiercely aiming his celestial bow Kodanda with the fiery Agneyastra missile to evaporate the ocean after Varuna failed to grant passage to Lanka. Ravi Varma captures intense kinetic drama: Rama's red dhoti billows violently in the oceanic gale, while his powerful muscular stance radiates righteous fury. In the churning background, translucent green waves crash in frothing white surf against dark boulders, as the terrified ocean god Varuna rises with his entourage of sea nymphs with folded hands, pleading for divine mercy. Through the Ravi Varma Lithographic Press established in 1894, such dramatic mythological visions were mass-produced as color oleographs, transforming the visual consciousness of modern India, conserved in the Sri Chitra Art Gallery, Thiruvananthapuram.
